#308842 298 2007-03-30T17:19:19Z sweep
Categories
This is what we ended up using last year, and what I suggest you use this year:
Action Map of the Year
DDA of the Year
Fan Programme of the Year
Map Maker of the Year
Map Series of the Year
Mare & Raigan Award for Contribution to the Community
Most Innovative Use of Objects or Tiles
N Art of the Year
N Player of the Year (In hindsight, this category is badly worded. I think some people were just voting for their favourite person. Maybe "Highscorer of the Year" would be clearer)
Puzzle Map of the Year
Race Map of the Year
Run of the Year
Survival Map of the Year
Tileset of the Year
The only category we scrapped last year was comic of the year, because it was a one-horse race between Dave and Dave. I don't think there needs to be any changes from the current set-up, but by all means, if you come up with something, go ahead and suggest.

HTML Voting & Nominations
I ran both the voting and nominations through a HTML form system last year, as I'm sure you're aware. I used Freedback, which is really simple to use, you need to coding knowledge at all. The only important thing is that when pasting the HTML code into your post you place it inside [html][/html] tags. I shouldn't think you'll have any problems with this, but if you do, feel free to ask. The form results will be stored on your Freedback account, and you can also have them sent to an email address. Freedback is free as long as you only ever do one form at a time, which obviously suffices for our needs.
Here's the most complicated bit: because Freedback cannot verify which user submitted the votes, you need to run a special system. It does tell you their IP, and as a member of staff you can match the username to the IP to check that things are in order. The only minor problem is if they're a NUMA user - I sort of used my best judgment on that.

Counting Votes & Nominations
Nominations: essentially I had a thread in this forum which I updated every now and again with all sensible nominations.
When it came to votes, I tallied it all up using Excel. The complications arose when people changed their votes. For this reason, I suggest you either tell people that when they vote it is final, or you make sure you keep a record of who voted what.

The M&R Award
I just PM'd them. They weren't hard to persuade, and just needed a small amount of polite prodding to get it done in time for the deadline.

Any questions?

Best Bitesize Map '07 - I think this would be a bit pointless. The reality is that all the best maps are bitesized (pretty much). This is equivalent to "Best Map of the Year" which we canned in favour for the Action category, so the N Hall of Fame could cover just maps in general.
Community Recognition Award - not a bad idea at all. How would this work? Would it be a category like the highscorer and player categories where there were no nominations, and people voted for whoever they wanted? Would this make the M&R Award less special? It _is_ a good idea though.

#394136 12 2007-12-28T16:26:33Z sweep
Quote: Limer, 2007-12-28T08:33:07Z
Also, illegal downloading is bad for the music business.
And i would still like for there to be one in the future
Myth. Don't believe everything the media tells you.

Firstly, when someone illegally downloading music, it's a "zero-sum" theft. If you steal a car, some poor bastard has lost his car. If you illegally download music, no-one physically loses it. This means there is only one loss for the music business - that's the potential business they could have got from you if your only option was to buy it.

This is obviously a bad thing if, say, someone would definitely have bought an album had the option to obtain it illegally not come up. But in many instances someone who gets their hands on music illegally would almost certainly not have considered buying the album in the first place. People are more likely to take a risk on music if it's free (obviously). In cases such as that the loss of business is minimal.

So, I'm saying they lose out, just not as much as you expect... but a loss is still a loss right? Well, yes. But an illegal download doesn't just result in a loss of potential business. It can also trigger a gain in potential business.

Let's say I download some obscure album by a band I've never heard of because I overheard someone in a bar talking about it, making it sound really great. Note that this probably wouldn't be enough for me to buy the album - but m,aybe enough to trigger a download. Well, I listen to it, and I decide I love it. I then play it to my friends. I tell other people on the net about it. I might even talk about it enthusiastically in bars! Some of these people go illegally download it... but some of them inevitably buy the album. Maybe I pay to see them live with my mates.
See how that worked out? The original loss was negligible - I'd never have the bought the album anyway. Then, out of nothing, came all this new revenue. Obviously my example is an extreme one, but you get the point. An illegal download is not necessarily bad for the music industry. They might even gain from it. There was even a Yale study into illegal downloading which came to the conclusion that the music industry made money out of illegal downloading.

Even if the big music labels are losing money, is that such a bad thing? Let them die on their feet. They rip off their artists, passing on an insulting proportion of revenue. The internet is perhaps triggering a huge change in the industry - big record labels are defunct in many ways, providing a band has the talent, and a way to get themselves out there, they stand a pretty damn good chance without a big company and marketing campaign behind them. Heck, if we take the record labels out of the equation, maybe we'd see a lot less terrible dirge filling up the radio. Less pre-packaged dirge, more raw talent.

It's all shifting more emphasis onto live music too. If there's more money on live music, artists are going to have to be quality, good enough to carry a live show - which can only be a good thing, surely.

Without illegal downloading, a lot of people would never have been exposed to such interesting, exciting, inventive music. Some of these are the future musicians of the world - maybe thanks to illegal downloading they will have been inspired in a way they wouldn't have been otherwise. Maybe these people will grow up and produce better music than would have happened without illegal downloading. I would argue that's how you should measure the music industry - not on profits & margins, but on the quality of the music. Music is an art. It should be treated as such.

So, yes. I think it's probably a good thing for the industry.

I would say, however...
1) Even if an artist is selling their music through the normal avenues, they may not be against illegal downloading. In fact, they might even see it as part of their business model - alongside the legal selling of the album.
2) Most people don't understand the true effects of illegal downloading. Artists within the industry are likely to have heard the same "bringing the industry to its knees" crap over and over again. They are likely to choose how to distribute their music on the basis of this false information. If I illegally download the music, I might well be doing him a lot of good in the long run. Is that really so bad, if their original decision was based on poor information in the first place?*

Now, don't get me wrong. I would never say that I am a good person because I illegally download music sometimes. It doesn't mean that I'm saving the music industry. In fact, from my point of view all it really means is that I can afford to do more with my life - including going to gigs & festivals. I don't think it makes me a bad person though - what I'm doing probably doesn't have an adverse effect on the people I think are of great value within the industry, and heck, I'm just enjoying my life as much as I can, without getting in anybody else's way.
It's just time for people to get realistic and understand the facts.

*Parallel: blind, deaf man about to cross a busy street, because he think it's a quiet one. What's wrong with me stopping him?

I like the way you put it, and your example does explain what you're trying to say, but I'll maintain it isn't really the same. What I'm saying, is that if illegal downloading has a tendency to create profit for the producer, then if thousands of people do it, it will average out to a profit.

The problem that I have with this is that there's nothing to show that tendency, in any form. There's only been the exact opposite shown.
My memories of looking up this stuff around about a year ago show that studies have found a tendency of profit. I decided to see if I could trace back any of this... true to the human mind, I have admittedly distorted the original message somewhat. Here's a passage which influenced me a lot, which I found saved in the dark places of my computer...
Quote
"Does illegal file-sharing cut into CD sales?"

According to a Harvard survey from March 2004 the damage developed from file-sharing tends to zero.
The principal reasons for decrease in revenue in the music industry are the same all over the world.
-Strong substitution of legal sales through non-authorized cd burnings.
-Stiff competition relative to decreasing leisure budget (expenses for other media)
-General uncertain business environment

"File-sharing increases welfare?"

Consumers are making as much profit as the price for the product lies under their individual willingness to pay.
Producers on the other hand only gain profit when they achieve a certain amount for their product which brings the marginal cost in.
In the case of the music industry it strikes that the latitude between marginal costs and selling price is extraordinary big. It costs about one dollar to produce a music-cd, but the consumer have to pay $15 or more. The very fact is that the margin broad in such a way is a sign that this market contains huge deadweight loss. If the CDs would be cheaper more of them would be sold and the consumer and producer together would have a bigger benefit.
One part of this deadweight loss is recoup by distribution of digital copies. If people dont want to pay $15 and download music from the internet than this is an utility from the economic field of view. In this situation a profit is attained. This profit is calculated between the difference of individual willingness from the music hearer and the marginal cost for copying the CD. Without this possibility of file-sharing this profit wouldnt be achieved.

Conclusion: File-sharing does not harm everyone. On the other side some get utility thereof. All in all we are better with file-sharing than without.

"The point of view of the artist"

With the quantity of circulating copies of an act the awareness level and the current market value of an artist is increasing. On top of that a spillover-effect arises. The bigger the awareness level the bigger are the potential earnings of an artist by the use of live gigs, engagements in advertisement or disposal of cell phone ring tones.
I'm standing by the assertion that I don't see the presence of illegal downloading as costly to the industry. But I'll back down on the idea that it is profitable in any significant manner, overall.

If it doesn't cost the industry money, does that mean it is morally correct? I don't know. The argument that you are violating other people's rights is a simple and very effective one. But if I came across a young teenager who was discovering all kinds of incredible music from all over the world, and was doing this by taking risks in what he listened to, I certainly wouldn't want to deny him the right to be doing so thanks to illegal downloading. I definitely wouldn't say his actions were deplorable.

#397659 66 2008-01-06T13:29:57Z sweep
Here's why you're confused: you've misread it. Those three points are not related to illegal downloading - they are simply stated as the three principle reasons for loss of revenue in the music industry. According to the Havard research.

Quote
Strong substitution of legal sales through non-authorized cd burnings.
Less CDs are sold, because more CDs are burned. There is no mention that illegal downloading is simply a substitute for CD burning - which is true, but only to a degree. It would only reduce harm done, if anything.

Quote: Kablizzy, 2008-01-05T21:33:15Z
Stiff competition relative to decreasing leisure budget (expenses for other media)
This is phrased in a way which puts my head in knots somewhat. I believe the general point is that the competition from other formats of media is increasing, relative to the music area of media.

Quote
General uncertain business environment
You say it isn't uncertain: I disagree. We're at a point where artists are abandoning the system and distributing in their own way, the importance of certain areas is shifting greatly (live music on the up etc.) and the internet and illegal downloading is shifting the industry into new territories. It is uncertain, because none of this has happened before, certainly not in this fashion.

Quote: Kablizzy, 2008-01-05T21:33:15Z
He's also right that if the CDs were cheaper to begin with, many more would be sold, but I fail to understand what bearing that has on illegal downloading.
The suggestion is that an increase in illegal downloading will force CDs to become cheaper, and this will favour the market as a whole. Either the overall consumer benefit from cheaper CDs will outweigh the overall producer loss, or both the producer and the consumer will ultimately gain.

consumer benefit - consumer loss + producer benefit - producer loss = overall benefit to the market = welfare gain

It's worth noting that this is arguing that even if the producer made a loss overall then the market could still gain. This is often how economists view markets - think of it what you will.

The second paragraph is simply with a view to how the consumer gains. It is arguing that what the consumer gains from an illegal download - the utility of one CD - is larger than what the producer loses (the potential for business). This doesn't even go into the realms of the domino effect of further profits down the line as a result.

As for the shaky conclusion, well, this is only the summary. I'm not sure if the whole thing is viewable online anywhere, but perhaps it would seem less shaky if you could view the entire research.
